title: Orbitlytics Incident Review - Rate Limiter False Positives

transcript.speaker: Derek Osei
transcript.text: Let's review Tuesday's incident - several customers got throttled with 429s even though they were well under the documented limit.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: Root cause was a bug in how we counted requests across our two API gateway nodes. Each node kept its own local count instead of a shared one, and the aggregation logic elsewhere read a stale merged count that was sometimes too high.

transcript.speaker: Jae-won Lee
transcript.text: Right - the shared count in Redis wasn't being refreshed on every request under high concurrency, there was a caching layer that held onto a stale value for up to 30 seconds. So a customer already using most of their quota looked like they'd blown through it.

transcript.speaker: Derek Osei
transcript.text: How many customers were affected and for how long?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: Fourteen customers saw at least one false 429 over a 40-minute window. Three of them were significant enough traffic that they filed support tickets.

transcript.speaker: Jae-won Lee
transcript.text: Short term, I've already increased the refresh frequency on that cache from 30 seconds to 2 seconds, which is deployed and reduces the odds of a stale read a lot. Longer term, I think we should remove the cache layer entirely for rate limit counts and read directly from Redis, accepting the small latency cost.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: I agree with removing the cache for correctness, but let's measure the latency impact first before deciding - if it adds real latency to every request, that's a tradeoff we should make deliberately, not by default.

transcript.speaker: Derek Osei
transcript.text: Agreed, let's decide that once we have real latency numbers, not today.

transcript.speaker: Jae-won Lee
transcript.text: I'll benchmark direct Redis reads under production-like load this week and bring numbers to the next sync.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: I'll also add an alert so we catch anomalous 429 rates going forward instead of relying on customers reporting it.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nandakumar
transcript.text: One open question - should we proactively credit or apologize to the three customers who filed tickets, or just respond to their tickets as normal?

transcript.speaker: Derek Osei
transcript.text: Let me loop in support and decide that separately, not in this review.

transcript.speaker: Derek Osei
transcript.text: Thanks both, good root cause work.

summary_key_points: A stale Redis cache for shared rate-limit counts caused false 429 errors for fourteen customers over 40 minutes
The immediate fix increased the cache refresh frequency from 30 seconds to 2 seconds
Whether to remove the cache layer entirely depends on latency benchmarks not yet run
An alert for anomalous 429 rates will be added so future incidents are caught proactively

action_items.task: Benchmark direct Redis reads under production-like load and bring numbers to the next sync
Add an alert for anomalous 429 rates

decisions: Decide whether to remove the rate-limit cache layer entirely only after seeing latency benchmark numbers
